lead: Entropy is the property that turns the second law into arithmetic. The Carnot cycle shows that δQ_rev/T sums to zero around any reversible loop, so that ratio depends only on the end states — it defines a state function S. Once you can compute ΔS, you can decide whether a process is possible, because the entropy of an isolated system never falls. Chemical engineers use this to test whether a proposed separation, heat-exchanger network or liquefaction train can work at all, and to measure how much work a real plant throws away.
prereq: You need: 3.3 Carnot cycle, the first law and the idea of a state function from Unit 1, and ideal-gas relations from Unit 2.

sections.h3: Entropy is a state function built from δQ_rev/T

blocks.text: In the Carnot cycle (see 3.3), heat Q_H enters at T_H and Q_C leaves at T_C. For a reversible cycle the efficiency is 1 − T_C/T_H, and the energy balance then gives Q_H/T_H = Q_C/T_C. Taking heat leaving as negative, the sum around the cycle is zero: Σ δQ_rev/T = 0.

Any reversible cycle can be sliced into thin Carnot strips, and each strip obeys the same result. So ∮δQ_rev/T = 0 for every reversible cycle. In Unit 1 you met the test: a quantity whose cyclic integral is zero is a state function, like internal energy. This one is called entropy, S.

blocks.where: dS is the change in entropy of the system (J/K); δQ_rev is the small heat added along a reversible path (J); T is the absolute temperature of the system in kelvin at which that heat crosses.

blocks.text: For a finite change, ΔS = ∫₁² δQ_rev/T, and the value depends only on states 1 and 2, never on the route. S is extensive, measured in J/K; per mole it is J/(mol·K), per kg J/(kg·K). Reversible heat divided by temperature is the whole definition — nothing about 'disorder' is needed at this level.

sections.h3: Calculating ΔS for the cases you meet

blocks.text: Because S is a state function, choose any convenient reversible path between the same two states. If the real path is irreversible, use a substitute path made of simple pieces.

blocks.where: C_V is the molar heat capacity at constant volume, J/(mol·K); R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) is the gas constant; V₁ and V₂ are initial and final volumes; T is in kelvin.

C_P is the molar heat capacity at constant pressure, J/(mol·K); P₁ and P₂ are initial and final pressures; T is in kelvin. The minus sign comes from the relation T dS = dH − V dP. For an ideal gas dH = C_P dT, so dividing by T gives dS = C_P dT/T − R dP/P; raising the pressure at constant T therefore lowers the entropy.

blocks.text: With constant heat capacity these integrate to ΔS = C_V ln(T₂/T₁) + R ln(V₂/V₁) and ΔS = C_P ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(P₂/P₁). For an isothermal ideal-gas expansion the temperature terms vanish and only the volume or pressure term survives.

blocks.where: ΔH is the latent heat of the phase change in J/mol at temperature T in K (melting, boiling or sublimation). The sign of ΔH carries the sign of ΔS.
the second form holds for a solid or liquid heated with constant C_P and no phase change; T₁ and T₂ are in kelvin.

items: Fix the end states and write down their T, P and V.
Break the path into constant-T, constant-P or constant-V pieces.
Apply the matching formula to each piece.
Add the pieces, keeping signs: melting is positive, condensation negative.

blocks.text: Real cycles are irreversible. Compare any such cycle with a reversible one working between the same two reservoirs at T_H and T_C. The real efficiency is lower, so Q_C/Q_H > T_C/T_H, and with rejected heat counted negative the cyclic integral drops below zero.

blocks.where: δQ is the heat crossing the system boundary (J); T is the absolute temperature of the reservoir or boundary where that heat crosses, in K; the integral runs over the whole cycle. Zero means a reversible cycle, negative means irreversible, positive is impossible.

blocks.text: This is the Clausius inequality. Some syllabi call it the mathematical statement of the second law, because it converts the words of 3.1 into a number you can evaluate for any proposed device.

blocks.where: the process form, for a change from state 1 to state 2; T is the temperature of the boundary where δQ crosses, in K. Equality holds only for a reversible path. When the boundary temperature is a constant T₀ this reduces to ΔS_system ≥ Q/T₀.

blocks.text: Now apply it to a system plus its surroundings at T₀. The surroundings exchange heat reversibly, so their entropy change is −Q/T₀, and the inequality rearranges to ΔS_system − Q/T₀ ≥ 0, that is, ΔS_universe ≥ 0. For an isolated system, ΔS ≥ 0, with equality only when everything inside is reversible.

blocks.where: S_gen is the entropy generated by irreversibility, J/K; it is zero for a reversible process and positive for every real one. The work lost because of it is the theme of 3.7.

figure.caption: A cyclic device feeds the Clausius integral. The result is zero for a reversible cycle, negative for an irreversible one, and a positive value is forbidden.

spec.title: Clausius inequality
spec.aria: A cyclic device feeds the Clausius integral; zero means reversible, negative means irreversible, and positive is impossible.

examples.question: One mole of an ideal gas at 300 K expands reversibly and isothermally from 10 L to 20 L. Find the heat added, the entropy change of the gas, and the entropy change of the surroundings.
steps: Reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas: ΔU = 0, so Q_rev = W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁).
ΔS_gas = Q_rev/T = 1728.8 J / 300 K = 5.76 J/K. Cross-check with R ln(V₂/V₁) = 8.314 × 0.6931 = 5.76 J/K.
The gas takes this heat from the reservoir, so ΔS_sur = −1728.8/300 = −5.76 J/K, and ΔS_universe = 0, as it must be for a reversible process.
examples.answer: Q_rev = 1728.8 J, ΔS of the gas = 5.76 J/K, and ΔS of the surroundings = −5.76 J/K.
examples.check:
import math
R = 8.314
T = 300.0
n = 1.0
V1, V2 = 10.0, 20.0
Q = n * R * T * math.log(V2 / V1)
print(round(Q, 1))
print(round(Q / T, 2))
print(round(-Q / T, 2))

traps: Using the real irreversible heat in dS = δQ/T. The actual Q/T is not the entropy change; compute ΔS along a reversible substitute between the same end states.
Putting the system temperature instead of the boundary temperature in ∮δQ/T. For an irreversible process the T belongs to the reservoir where the heat crosses.
Swapping the signs of the two ideal-gas forms: the volume term is +R ln(V₂/V₁), the pressure term is −R ln(P₂/P₁). Using plus with pressure gives the wrong sign in compression.
Forgetting that freezing and condensation have negative ΔS, because their ΔH is negative and ΔS = ΔH/T keeps that sign.
Unit slip: R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) with T in kelvin. Writing 0.08314 L·bar/(mol·K) leaves the answer in L·bar/K, not J/K.

quiz.q: Define the entropy change for a reversible path.
quiz.a: dS = δQ_rev/T, so ΔS = ∫₁² δQ_rev/T along any reversible path between the states. Unit: J/K.

quiz.q: Why does ∮δQ_rev/T = 0 prove that entropy is a state function?
quiz.a: A quantity whose integral around every closed path is zero depends only on the end states. That is the definition of a state function, so S can be tabulated like U and H.

quiz.q: Two moles of an ideal gas are heated at constant volume from 300 K to 600 K. Find ΔS. C_V = 12.5 J/(mol·K).
One mole of saturated water vapour condenses at 373 K and 1 atm. ΔH_vap = 40.66 kJ/mol. Find ΔS.
quiz.a: Condensation releases heat, so ΔH = −40 660 J/mol. ΔS = ΔH/T = −40 660/373 = −109 J/(mol·K).

quiz.q: A cycle takes 100 kJ from a 500 K reservoir, delivers 30 kJ of work and rejects 70 kJ to a 300 K reservoir. Evaluate ∮δQ/T and comment.
quiz.a: ∮δQ/T = 100/500 − 70/300 = 0.200 − 0.2333 = −0.0333 kJ/K. Negative, so the cycle is irreversible but possible; a positive value would make it impossible.

quiz.q: An inventor claims a cycle takes 500 kJ from a 400 K reservoir, rejects 400 kJ to a 300 K reservoir and delivers 100 kJ of work. Test the claim.
quiz.a: Energy balances: 500 − 400 = 100 kJ, so the first law is satisfied. ∮δQ/T = 500/400 − 400/300 = 1.25 − 1.333 = −0.0833 kJ/K, which is negative. The claim survives; the cycle is simply irreversible, with 20% efficiency against the Carnot 25%.

quiz.q: What does the Clausius inequality say for an isolated system?
quiz.a: Start from the process form derived in Section 3, ΔS_system − Q/T₀ ≥ 0. An isolated system exchanges no heat, so Q = 0 and this gives ΔS_isolated ≥ 0, with equality only when every change inside is reversible. Note that the cyclic integral ∮δQ/T ≤ 0 is a statement about a cycle: put Q = 0 there and it reads 0 ≤ 0, which tells you nothing. Do not treat ∮δQ/T as the same object as ΔS; the cyclic form and the process form are separate statements.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, ΔS values come from steam tables and equation-of-state software rather than hand integrals, which is where Unit 4, Thermodynamic Property Relations, takes over. Entropy generation is the working currency of exergy analysis, used to size heat-recovery networks and to audit plants for wasted work. Newer curricula also tie ΔS to information theory and to the statistical picture in 3.10. Useful search terms: exergy analysis, entropy generation number, Gouy–Stodola theorem.
